slides.title: Chapter 12: Command Line Programs
slides.say: Welcome. This chapter follows a typed command to a running program: the terminal, PATH, a virtual environment, the arguments, the look of the output, and the launcher. Every code slide shows the code, a plain explanation and the result drawn as a table, chart or diagram.

slides.title: Today's route
slides.say: Five parts: starting a program, isolating it, letting it read its surroundings, designing its text output, and deploying it. Each code slide has its place in the chapter-code tab of the page, in this same order.

slides.title: Two questions this chapter answers
slides.say: Two questions to carry through the chapter. How does a typed command become a running program, and how does the program learn what it was given? And which outputs and launchers of the book differ in current Python?

slides.title: Part 1: Starting a program
slides.say: Part one. Programs have many names. The terminal finds a program by searching the folders of PATH, from left to right. Predict which folder wins before you read the result.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: starting a program
slides.say: A drive-through is a good picture for the terminal: short orders, text answers. A command line program is a button on a vending machine. Ask students to add one more everyday picture of their own.

slides.title: A Program by Any Other Name
slides.say: Seven words for nearly the same thing. A script is run from source by an interpreter. A command is a program you start from a terminal. Ask students which word fits their last project.

slides.title: The terminal: cd and pwd as Python calls
slides.say: The terminal commands cd and pwd have Python twins: os.chdir and os.getcwd. We run them in a throw-away folder. Predict what pwd prints inside Desktop.

slides.title: The terminal: ls and dir *.exe as Python calls
slides.say: Ls and dir have one twin: os.listdir. The filter keeps names that end in dot exe, like dir star dot exe. Predict how many names each command shows.

slides.title: PATH: a text of folders, searched in order
slides.say: PATH is just text. The terminal splits it at the colons and tries the folders in order. A folder put first wins. Predict the number of folders before you run it.

slides.title: which: the first folder that holds the program
slides.say: Shutil.which does the same walk the terminal does and returns the first hit. Who wins when two folders hold spam? And what does it return when nothing matches?

slides.title: Part 2: Isolating a program
slides.say: Part two. A virtual environment keeps one project's packages apart from the rest. pip installs into exactly the Python you name. Notice how little a venv really is: a folder and a file.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: environments and packages
slides.say: A lunch box keeps your food apart from the shared kitchen, just as a virtual environment keeps your packages apart. Pip is the order form for new packages.

slides.title: Virtual environments: a folder and a settings file
slides.say: A virtual environment is a folder with a small settings file and three parts: bin, lib and pyvenv.cfg. Each line of the file is one setting, so a dictionary can read it.

slides.title: activate puts the environment first on PATH
slides.say: Activate only changes PATH, for one terminal window. The test sys.prefix not equal to sys.base_prefix tells a program whether it runs inside an environment.

slides.title: pip: pin a version, find a module
slides.say: Pip pins a version with two equals signs. Run pip as python dash m pip, so it installs into the Python you mean. Find_spec asks whether a module can be imported before you try.

slides.title: Story: pip began as pyinstall, September 2008
slides.say: Ian Bicking announced pyinstall on 24 September 2008 and renamed it pip a month later. PEP 405 then made virtual environments part of Python 3.3. The two commands of this part are his two ideas side by side.

slides.title: Part 3: Programs that look around
slides.say: Part three. A program can ask about its system, its version and its file, and it can read the words after its name. argparse does that reading for you and refuses wrong input.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: programs that know themselves
slides.say: Four small ideas. The program checks its surroundings, reads the words it was given, lets argparse fill the form, and leaves a clear note when it must stop.

slides.title: Self-aware programs: system, version, file
slides.say: A program can ask which family of system, which Python version and whether it came from a file. Dunder file is an absolute path since Python 3.9. Predict each answer.

slides.title: Missing modules and sys.exit with a message
slides.say: Catch ModuleNotFoundError and explain in your own words. Sys.exit with a text ends the program, prints the text to standard error and gives exit code 1. Here we catch it to show the value.

slides.title: Command line arguments: sys.argv
slides.say: The shell splits the line into words, and quotation marks keep two words together. Sys.argv holds the words, with the script name first. Predict the length of each list.

slides.title: argparse: declare the arguments once
slides.say: Once arguments multiply, declare them once with argparse. It converts types and fills in defaults. Predict the density for the second run.

slides.title: argparse: a wrong word is refused
slides.say: A word that is not a number is refused by the int conversion. Argparse turns that into one clear message. In a terminal the exit code would be 2.

slides.title: Part 4: Designing the terminal output
slides.say: Part four. A text program is designed for being typed and read. Quiet by default, colour by escape code, block characters for pictures. The snowstorm puts them together.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: how a program looks and sounds
slides.say: Text design in nine pictures. Notice that the pop-up and the sound are the two ways to interrupt a person. Use them only when you must.

slides.title: Text-based design: quiet by default
slides.say: Quiet by default is the Unix habit. The minus v switch asks for more and minus q for none. The bars show how many lines each mode prints.

slides.title: Story: the pipe and the quiet command, 1973
slides.say: Doug McIlroy proposed the pipe in 1964 and Ken Thompson built it in one night in 1973. The 1978 maxims say: do not clutter output. That is why a command is quiet by default. Ask: who reads your program's output?

slides.title: Story: a text screen that felt like a desktop, 1986
slides.say: Norton Commander shipped in 1986 with two panels drawn only with characters. The chapter's Figure 12-1 shows it. Our snowstorm is the same idea with block characters. Ask students what else a text screen could show.

slides.title: Terminal presentation: chr and os.system
slides.say: Os.system hands a text to the shell. Cls on Windows, clear elsewhere. Chr turns a number into a character. The three block characters are the snow and the ground.

slides.title: Colour in the terminal: what bext.fg and bext.bg send
slides.say: Bext sets colours with names, but the terminal receives escape codes: 30 to 37 for text, 40 to 47 for background. This stand-in builds the same codes. Zero resets.

slides.title: Pop-ups, sound and colour: the helpers
slides.say: Three of these helpers are not in the standard library. Pymsgbox needs Tkinter, bext needs a terminal and playsound needs a sound system. That is why the page does not run them.

slides.title: Snowstorm: one frame of the animation
slides.say: The snowstorm decides cell by cell whether there is snow. The density comes from the argument. The book clears the screen and repeats the frame; we print one seeded frame and count the flakes.

slides.title: Part 5: Deploying a program
slides.say: Part five. A program becomes a command when a launcher sits in a PATH folder. We build the Ubuntu launcher, two small programs that touch the system, and a bundle with PyInstaller.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: deploying
slides.say: Deploying means reachable by name. Ccwd and the recorder are two tiny programs that touch the system. PyInstaller packs the interpreter along, so the file is large.

slides.title: Launcher files on three systems
slides.say: One idea, three spellings. Windows uses a bat file and percent star. macOS and Linux use a shell script and dollar at in quotes. Forward the arguments, or the script never sees them.

slides.title: Deploying on Ubuntu: the launcher script
slides.say: The launcher starts with the hash-bang line, activates the environment and runs the script with all its arguments. Three lines, three jobs.

slides.title: Deploying on Ubuntu: chmod u+x
slides.say: Chmod u plus x is what makes the file a command: the owner gets the x bit. Which then finds it by its bare name on PATH.

slides.title: Story: the #! line, announced by email, 1980
slides.say: Dennis Ritchie announced the hash-bang line by email on 10 January 1980. Our Ubuntu launcher starts with it. Ask students why the file needs no dot sh ending.

slides.title: Deploying on Ubuntu: the .desktop entry
slides.say: A desktop file is a small settings file. Configparser reads it. The Exec line is the launcher, wrapped in a terminal window so that the user sees the output.

slides.title: ccwd: copying the current working directory
slides.say: Os.chdir changes the folder of the running program only. The terminal that started it stays where it was. That is the chapter's point, and why ccwd copies the folder instead of moving there.

slides.title: Clipboard Recorder: print what changed
slides.say: The recorder polls again and again and prints only what changed. Control-C raises KeyboardInterrupt, which is not an Exception, so the except clause names it. It ends quietly.

slides.title: PyInstaller: one file, a whole interpreter
slides.say: Pyinstaller needs its capital letters and two dashes. Python dash m Pyinstaller dash dash onefile builds one executable. It leaves build, dist and a spec file.

slides.title: PyInstaller: what the one file costs
slides.say: Pyinstaller packs a copy of the interpreter with the script, so even Hello world is megabytes. The output belongs to one operating system and one Python version. Mail providers may block it.

slides.title: Practice program: make your programs deployable
slides.say: The practice program turns four old projects into commands. One template serves all. The only change per project is its name in the third line.

slides.title: Current Python and systems change more
slides.say: Python moves on. Dunder file is absolute since 3.9. No setuptools in new environments since 3.12. Python 3.13 adds a gitignore file. Python 3.14 colours argparse help. PEP 668 blocks pip in system Python.

slides.title: Summary
slides.say: Five sentences to keep. The chart counts the code examples in each part of this deck.

slides.title: Practice Questions
slides.say: Four drills. Predict first, then run what you can on the page. Ask students to explain each answer in one sentence.

slides.title: Resources: where to go next
slides.say: Start with the book chapter, then the Python documentation, the two PEPs and the pip and PyInstaller manuals. The stories link to first-hand sources. Choose one link and read it before the next class.
